newsitem.title: UK: Freight agents' group fears another Lockerbie.
newsitem.headline: Freight agents' group fears another Lockerbie.

text.p: A terrorist bombing attack on a commercial airliner is still a possibility despite air cargo security regulations in effect in Britain, warned the British freight forwarders' association, BIFA.

Roger Blacklock, air division head of the British International Freight Association, told Reuters the Aviation Security (Air Cargo Regulations) 1993 were "inadequate." Until they were improved, "possibility for terrorist attack remains."

Britain's Department of Transport (DoT) said it was "sympathetic" to BIFA's views and promised to review the situation. A spokeswoman said the DoT would consider any options it is offered concerning changes to the law.
Since the Regulations were passed in Parliament, 18 'listed' agents have been 'de-listed' for failure to meet DoT requirements.
The DoT also has the power to prosecute errant agents, but has yet to do so, Blacklock said.
In December 1988, on Pan Am flight 103, a terrorist bomb exploded as the plane passed over Lockerbie, Scotland, killing 270 people.
The bomb was found to have been planted in a suitcase in the bellyhold. About two-thirds of the world's air cargo is flown in the bellyhold of aircraft.

This resulted in the 1993 Regulations, which Blacklock said were drafted as a "political" move without consulting with freight forwarders, who are now legally responsible for ensuring that airfreight shipments are safe and secure.
Under the law, which came into effect in August 1994, the DoT grants forwarders 'listed' agent status after their premises and operations are vetted and classified as secure by the department.
There are now 497 'listed' agents in Britain legally responsible for the security of the cargo provided by their shipper customers, mainly exporters.

"The fundamental weak link in this regime is that only forwarders are legally responsible for their shippers' and sub-contractors' (truckers and independent warehouse operators for example) shipments," said Blacklock.
He said some 'listed' agents were accepting cargo shipments from mainly small "backstreet, under-the-arches" shippers without vetting their sometimes dubious security measures.

"These forwarders are doing this for commercial reasons. They are doing it not for the sake of security but to get business from the small shipper who may, for example, provide them with one-tonne of freight a month to Timbuktu or wherever," Blacklock said."And the Department of Transport knows this is going on."

He urged the DoT to press to alter the 1993 Regulations to make shippers and their sub-contractors legally responsible for security of cargo while in their possession, with forwarders taking on the liability on receipt or collection of consignments.
Blacklock said he would present a paper outlining BIFA's views to the UK Air Freight Forum, comprising airlines, shippers and forwarders, at that organisation's next meeting here on September 16.
He said he expected proposals to change the law would be passed on to the government soon afterwards and said "if the act is changed by next year, we would be more than happy."
He said any change in the present law depended on the level of urgency and priority the new Labour government placed on aviation security.
